rank.idea: Bias slightly toward leaving a moderate remainder for mid-size items to preserve very small bins for later, without needing future-item lookahead.
Use a light nonlinear penalty on leftover space (e.g., quadratic in remainder) to distinguish among near-ties while still behaving like best-fit.
Add a small exact-fit / divisibility bonus on top of best-fit so bins leaving remainder 0, 5, or 10 are preferred when slack is otherwise similar.

Introduce a lightweight competitiveness term that approximates future flexibility from the current slack alone: prefer placements that either exactly fill a bin or leave a remainder near a 'hub' region of reusable capacities, and otherwise bias toward the bin whose post-placement remainder is closest to the median feasible remainder among all bins. This creates a global shaping effect without looking ahead, helping break ties among equally tight bins and reducing the chance of creating isolated leftovers.

Use a two-regime score that adapts to item size: for large items, strongly prefer minimum slack (best-fit behavior) to avoid future infeasibility; for small items, add a mild anti-fragmentation preference that preserves medium-capacity bins by steering tiny items into either near-perfect fills or clearly large bins. Implement this with a smooth function of item/capacity and slack, not hard thresholds, so it generalizes across both capacity-150 and capacity-100 mixes.

Score bins by a combination of residual tightness and residual portability: reward placements that leave a remainder close to common item sizes implied by the training distributions (around 20–100 for uniform, around 20–60 with a long lower tail for Weibull), while penalizing remainders that are awkwardly small but not zero. This encourages leaving bins with capacities that are likely reusable, rather than creating many medium-sized stranded gaps.

Use a normalized scarcity heuristic: score each feasible bin by how scarce the resulting remainder would be under the known item distributions. Estimate scarcity with a simple piecewise function that penalizes remainders too small to be useful and also remainders in overrepresented ranges, while rewarding residuals that sit just above common item sizes. Combine with a strong exact-fit term and a slight preference for smaller residuals when bins are otherwise similar.

rank.idea: Introduce bin-usage awareness in the score: unused bins get a small but nonzero opening penalty, while already-open bins receive a mild bonus based on how well the post-placement remainder matches a compact set of desirable slack bands. This can reduce unnecessary bin openings without sacrificing fit quality, especially on the mixed-capacity settings.

Use a two-regime score: for large items, strongly prefer near-tight fits to preserve large bins; for small/medium items, blend tightness with a learned-from-distribution remainder preference that targets residuals near likely future item sizes (e.g., around the Weibull mode and around common round-number gaps). Implement as a vectorized sum of smooth kernels over residuals plus an exact-fit spike.

Hybrid tight-fit + remainder-shaping: start from best-fit (small residual is good), but add smooth bonuses for residuals that match likely future item sizes in both benchmarks, with different peaks for the two distributions and a stronger exact-fit reward. Use an item-size gate so large items remain mostly pure tight-fit while smaller items exploit future-friendly gaps.

Two-scale bin preservation heuristic: combine a short-term rule that prefers minimizing immediate waste with a medium-term rule that avoids creating residuals in the least useful middle band. For the OR-style case, bias toward leaving 20–50-ish remainders; for the Weibull case, bias toward small-to-mid remainders but penalize awkward large leftovers. Blend the terms by item-to-capacity ratio so the policy smoothly transitions from aggressive packing for large items to distribution-aware packing for smaller ones.

Capacity-aware scarcity penalty: favor bins whose remaining capacity is relatively rare among feasible bins, so the heuristic preserves versatile medium gaps and consumes uncommon near-perfect gaps only when the item is large enough. This can be implemented with fast vectorized counts/histogram-style terms over the current feasible capacities.

Two-regime residual shaping: keep best-fit as the base score, but add a small capacity-dependent bonus landscape that activates only when the item is relatively small versus the current bin capacity; use different residual peaks for the two training distributions (uniform/large-capacity vs Weibull/smaller-capacity) so the same function biases toward complements that are likely to be reused soon.

Robust hybrid tie-breaking via fit quality and leftover granularity: start from negative residual, then add a lightweight preference for exact fits, near-exact fits, and residuals that land in a few reusable 'granularity bands' (different bands for the two capacities); this combines strict first-fit behavior with a learned preference for leftovers that can absorb future items without overfitting to one distribution.

Open-bin discrimination with soft penalties: treat the preallocated unused bins as a separate class by detecting the maximum capacity and applying a mild penalty to unused bins unless they are near-perfect fits or clearly better than all used bins; this discourages wasteful bin opening while still allowing opening when the residual gain is substantial.
Use a single vectorized score that blends best-fit pressure with a lightweight complement-target bump around the empirically useful residual bands for each distribution.
Add a mild capacity-dependent penalty for leaving very small remainders in large-capacity bins, so the heuristic avoids creating awkward fragments in the 150-capacity regime.
Keep the same gated two-regime structure, but simplify the shaped bonuses to fewer terms and stronger exact-fit handling for speed and robustness.
